# Stair design principles

## Historical background

**Historical Approach.** The classical stair-design relationship is commonly expressed as "the Blondel value":

$$
2R + G \approx L
$$

where `R` is the rise and `G` is the going. Originally, Blondel introduce^["Blondel probably referred to the French (pre-Revolutionary) royal inch" (Templer, 1992, p. 27).] an ideal value of 64.77 cm (Templer, 1992, p. 27). 

The modern "Blondel's law" introduce the ideal value at 63 cm, with acceptable range of solution between 60 cm to 64 cm. 

**European Norms.** Regarding ISO standards, the European acceptable values are between 58 cm and 66 cm (ISO 14122-3:2016, NF EN ISO 14122-3:2017). Pour les parties communes et ERP, la réglementation indique un minimum de 60 cm. Thus, acceptable values are between 60 cm and 66 cm. 

Le giron doit être compris entre 21 cm and 31 cm (EN ISO 14122-3:2016, Safety of machinery - Permanent means of access to machinery - Part 3: Stairs, stepladders and guard-rails^[French equivalent to EN ISO 14122-3:2016 is NF EN ISO 14122-3:2017.]).

La hauteur maximum de marche est de 21 cm. Le giron minimal de 19 cm.

**French Norms.** Pour le DTU français, il y a 3 classes de confort d'escaliers:

1. Raide 1.32 > H/G > 1
2. Courant 1 > H/G > 0.78
3. Confortable H/G < 0.78

Avec H hauteur de marche et G Giron.

**Modern Approach.** Therefore, modern approach have the possibility to enlarge that theoritical value: 

> If we adjust for the pace of people today, depending on leg length and walking speed—say, 28 inches (71 cm) - and express the formula in today’s measures, then it would become: 

$$
2R + G \approx 71\ cm
$$

> Templer, John A. The Staircase: Studies of Hazards, Falls, and Safer Design. 2. print. *MIT Press*, 1992. https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/6434.001.0001. p. 27

**Experimental Research.**

Experimental research has subsequently investigated stair dimensions
using several criteria, including energy expenditure, biomechanical
constraints, perceived difficulty and fall risk. 

> A reasonable compromise would be a stair with risers
that are not less than 6.3 inches (16 cm) to suit ascent, and risers not more than 7.2 inches (18.3 cm) and goings greater than 9 inches (22.9 cm) to suit descent (Templer, 1992, p. 39).

> • In terms of gait, risers should be 6.3 to 7.2 inches (16-18.3 cm) and goings should not be less than 9 inches (22.9 cm).
> 
> • The etiological studies suggest that risers should not exceed 7.5 inches (19.1 cm) and goings should not be less than 9 inches (22.9 cm).
> 
> • To accommodate feet adequately, goings should not be less than 11 inches (27.9 cm).
> 
> Templer, John A. The Staircase: Studies of Hazards, Falls, and Safer Design. 2. print. *MIT Press*, 1992. https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/6434.001.0001. p. 38
